content: [{"order":1,"type":"heading","text":"Master-Replica Replication Mechanics and PSYNC in Redis"},{"order":2,"type":"subheading","text":"Introduction to Redis Replication"},{"order":3,"type":"paragraph","text":"Redis replication is a fundamental feature for achieving high availability, read scalability, and fault tolerance. By default, Redis uses a single-master architecture where data flows asynchronously from a master instance to one or more replica instances."},{"order":4,"type":"subheading","text":"The PSYNC Command Mechanics"},{"order":5,"type":"paragraph","text":"Historically, Redis used the SYNC command, which always triggered a full synchronization. Modern Redis versions (4.0 and above) use PSYNC (Partial Synchronization). PSYNC optimizes the replication process by attempting to send only the missing data stream when a replica reconnects after a temporary disconnection."},{"order":6,"type":"subheading","text":"Key Components of PSYNC"},{"order":7,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Master Run ID: Every Redis instance generates a unique 40-character pseudo-random hexadecimal string when it boots up. Replicas remember the run ID of their master."},{"order":8,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Replication Offset: A cumulative byte counter that increments as data is written to the master and propagated to replicas. Both the master and replica track this offset."},{"order":9,"type":"bullet_point","text":"Replication Backlog: A circular FIFO buffer maintained on the master. It stores recently propagated write commands along with their starting offsets."},{"order":10,"type":"subheading","text":"Full Resynchronization vs. Partial Resynchronization"},{"order":11,"type":"paragraph","text":"When a replica connects to a master, it issues a PSYNC command using the master's run ID and its last known replication offset. The master evaluates the request and responds with one of two outcomes:"},{"order":12,"type":"bullet_point","text":"FULLRESYNC: Triggered if the master run ID has changed (indicating a failover or restart) or if the replica's requested offset is no longer available in the replication backlog. The master generates an RDB file, sends it to the replica, and then streams the ongoing buffer."},{"order":13,"type":"bullet_point","text":"CONTINUE: Triggered if the master run ID matches and the requested offset falls within the range of the replication backlog. The master simply streams the missing bytes to the replica."},{"order":14,"type":"subheading","text":"Configuring the Replication Backlog"},{"order":15,"type":"paragraph","text":"To prevent unnecessary full resynchronizations during network blips, you must properly size the replication backlog. This is configured in the redis.conf file using the following parameters:"},{"order":16,"type":"code","text":"repl-backlog-size 1mb\nrepl-backlog-ttl 3600"},{"order":17,"type":"paragraph","text":"The repl-backlog-size defines the memory buffer allocated for holding data changes. A larger backlog handles longer network outages. The repl-backlog-ttl determines how many seconds to wait after the last replica disconnects before freeing the backlog memory."},{"order":18,"type":"subheading","text":"Conclusion"},{"order":19,"type":"paragraph","text":"Understanding PSYNC, replication offsets, and the replication backlog is critical for maintaining robust Redis clusters. Proper tuning ensures minimal network overhead and fast recovery times during network partitions."}]
